answer.rationale: The contract deadline is tight and the line has zero buffer (94% of committed volume), so any delivery disruption is high-cost. Memory c2 shows the low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply with quick onboarding, but the record is silent on sustained delivery performance under demand pressure or during a shortage—exactly the risk that matters here given no buffer. Memory c4 shows that benchmarking-driven renegotiation with the incumbent recovered real margin and improved terms without any switching or integration risk, which directly addresses the finance mandate while preserving the stability memory c1 also documents. Before committing, I want to verify c4's original record to confirm the magnitude of savings achieved via negotiation (to see if it could plausibly hit 18%) and verify c2's original record to check whether any delivery-risk caveats were omitted in consolidation. Given the primary objective is minimizing TCO without increasing delivery risk, and switching vendors this close to expiry with no integration buffer is the highest-risk option, negotiating with the incumbent first is the safer, reversible move—if it can't reach the mandate, switching or second-sourcing remains available next cycle. This is scaled as a standard experiment (full renegotiation of the primary contract) rather than a broad rollout, since it doesn't foreclose future switching, and rather than a tiny guarded test, since the contract itself is the full scope of this cycle's one decision.
